subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: In a play script, what is a stage direction?
options: An instruction about action, movement, setting or delivery, usually in brackets or italics
A line that the main character speaks aloud
A summary of the plot at the start of the script
A note written by the audience after the show
questions.explanation: Stage directions are the playwright's instructions about what happens on stage, such as movement, sound, lighting or how a line is delivered. They are not spoken.

questions.content: Which term describes a character speaking their private thoughts aloud to the audience while alone on stage?
options: Soliloquy
Aside
Prologue
Epilogue
questions.explanation: A soliloquy is a speech made by a character alone on stage, revealing inner thoughts. An aside is a brief remark to the audience while others are present.

questions.content: An invented script reads: LENA (whispering, glancing at the door) I never told him where the key was. What do the words in brackets tell an actor?
options: How to deliver the line and what to do while speaking
Which words to leave out
Where the interval should happen
What the audience should think about the writer
questions.explanation: The brackets give delivery (whispering) and action (glancing at the door), which suggest nerves or secrecy.

questions.content: What is dramatic irony?
options: The audience knows something that one or more characters do not
A character says the opposite of what they mean
A character speaks directly to the audience
The scene changes without a pause
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony depends on a gap in knowledge between the audience and the characters. Saying the opposite of what is meant is verbal irony.

questions.content: What does a prop in a play refer to?
options: A movable object used by actors on stage
The painted background of the set
The costume worn by the lead actor
The first line of the script
questions.explanation: A prop is a portable object handled by actors, such as a letter, a cup or a suitcase. Scenery is the set; clothing is costume.

questions.content: In an invented play, the stage direction reads: The lights fade slowly until only a single bulb above the empty chair remains lit. What is the most likely effect?
options: It focuses attention on absence and loneliness
It signals a joyful celebration
It shows that the scene takes place at noon
It shows that the actors have forgotten their lines
questions.explanation: Isolating one light on an empty chair draws the eye to what is missing, creating a mood of loneliness or loss.

questions.content: A character says to another, "Of course I trust you," and then turns to the audience and mutters, "As much as I trust a fox with the hens." What technique is the second remark?
options: An aside
A soliloquy
A flashback
A chorus
questions.explanation: A brief remark to the audience while other characters are present (and supposedly cannot hear) is an aside. A soliloquy is a longer speech when alone.

questions.content: In an invented scene, Omar celebrates his friend's surprise party plans while the audience has just seen the friend packing to leave town forever. What effect does this dramatic irony create?
options: Tension and sadness, because the audience senses the plans will fail
Confusion about who the characters are
Humour only, since nothing is at stake
A sense that the play is ending
questions.explanation: Because the audience knows more than Omar, his cheerfulness becomes poignant and builds suspense about when he will find out.

questions.content: Which stage direction would most clearly suggest that a character is hiding anger?
options: (smiling tightly, gripping the back of the chair)
(sitting comfortably and humming)
(walking offstage)
(pouring a glass of water)
questions.explanation: A tight smile combined with a gripping hand shows a gap between outward calm and inner feeling. The others show no tension.

questions.content: A playwright writes a long monologue in which a king, alone at night, admits he doubts his right to rule. Why might the playwright use a soliloquy here?
options: To give the audience access to his true feelings that he hides from others
To introduce the stage crew
To move the play to a new location
To make the other characters seem less important by accident
questions.explanation: Soliloquies reveal inner conflict honestly. That is why they are used for private doubts a character would not share publicly.

questions.content: In an invented play, a bare stage has only a long table and two chairs. A student writes that this "shows the play is unfinished". Which response is the strongest improvement?
options: The minimal set focuses attention on the dialogue and suggests an uncomfortable, formal confrontation
The set is plain because the play is cheap to make
Tables and chairs are the most common objects in plays
The set shows that the characters are poor
questions.explanation: A strong answer links a staging choice to its effect on meaning and mood. The other options are guesses with no supporting reasoning.

questions.content: Read this invented extract. NORA: (placing the letter on the table, without looking up) You may read it, if you like. JAMES: (does not move) Later. (A clock ticks. Neither speaks.) What does the pause with the ticking clock most likely emphasise?
options: Unspoken tension between the characters
That the scene takes place at a clock-maker's
That James has finished reading the letter
That Nora is about to leave the stage permanently
questions.explanation: Silence filled by a ticking clock makes time feel heavy and highlights what the characters will not say.

questions.content: Why do playwrights sometimes use a chorus or narrator who steps outside the action?
options: To comment on events, give background or guide the audience's response
To replace all the actors
To make the play shorter by removing the plot
To prove that the characters are not real
questions.explanation: A chorus or narrator can summarise, comment and shape how the audience judges events, adding a viewpoint beyond the characters.

questions.content: An invented stage direction says: (MARA exits. The door closes. The stage stays lit for a long moment, empty, as the radio softly plays a cheerful song.) A student claims the cheerful song is a mistake. Which interpretation best explains it?
options: Contrast between the happy music and the empty stage heightens the sense of loss
The radio is there to show the play is set in the present
Cheerful music always means the scene is humorous
The song fills time while the actors rest
questions.explanation: Juxtaposing cheerful sound with emptiness is an ironic contrast that makes the departure feel sadder. Dramatic choices usually do work for meaning.

questions.content: Which comment about stage directions shows the most insight when analysing a printed script?
options: They show the playwright's intentions about tone, and different productions may interpret them differently
They must be followed identically by every director
They are always less important than dialogue
They are only there to tell the actors when to enter
questions.explanation: Stage directions reveal intended mood and meaning, but directors and actors still make interpretive choices. Saying they are unimportant or fixed ignores that.

questions.content: In an invented play, two characters argue politely over tea while the stage direction notes that the cups rattle in their saucers. How does this detail work on the audience?
options: It reveals physical anxiety that contradicts their calm words
It shows the tea is too hot to drink
It tells the audience the play is a comedy
It suggests the stage floor is uneven
questions.explanation: The rattling is an involuntary action that exposes feelings the dialogue hides. The contrast between speech and action builds subtext.

questions.content: A student writes: "The playwright uses a spotlight on Daniel when he says he is fine." Which sentence best develops this into analysis?
options: The isolating spotlight exposes him, so the audience can see the strain behind his insistence that he is fine
The spotlight is bright and Daniel is on stage
Spotlights are used in many plays
Daniel says he is fine so the writer included a spotlight
questions.explanation: Strong analysis names the technique, explains its effect and links it to meaning (the contradiction between words and feelings). The others only describe or repeat.

questions.content: In an invented scene, a character's stage direction reads: (She folds the telegram into smaller and smaller squares as he speaks.) What does this action suggest, and what term describes unspoken meaning like this?
options: Growing distress; it is subtext shown through action
Boredom; it is dramatic irony
Excitement; it is a soliloquy
Confusion; it is a prologue
questions.explanation: Fidgeting with the telegram shows rising distress that she does not say aloud. Meaning carried beneath the words is called subtext.

note:
## What are dramatic techniques?
A play script is written to be performed, so a playwright has tools that a novelist does not. Dramatic techniques are the choices that shape how a play looks, sounds and feels to an audience. When you read a script in an exam, you are reading the blueprint for a performance, and good readers imagine that performance.

## Stage directions
Stage directions are instructions to actors and directors. They usually appear in brackets or italics and are not spoken. They can describe:
- **Action and movement**: (she steps back, then forward again) shows hesitation.
- **Delivery**: (whispering), (coldly), (through clenched teeth) guide tone.
- **Setting and props**: a cracked mirror, an empty chair, a locked door.
- **Lighting and sound**: a fading light, a distant siren, silence.
In a short extract, every stage direction is there for a reason. Ask: what does this tell me about feelings that the words do not?

## Key techniques
- **Soliloquy**: a speech by a character alone on stage, revealing private thoughts.
- **Aside**: a quick remark to the audience that other characters are not supposed to hear.
- **Monologue**: a long speech by one character, often to others.
- **Dramatic irony**: the audience knows something a character does not, which builds tension or sympathy.
- **Subtext**: the meaning beneath the words. A character may say "I'm fine" while their actions say otherwise.
- **Chorus or narrator**: a voice outside the action that comments or guides.
- **Props, costume and set**: objects and visuals that carry symbolic meaning.
- **Lighting and sound**: used to shape mood, focus attention and mark time or place.
- **Silence and pause**: deliberately used to show tension, shock or what cannot be said.

## From technique to effect
Examiners reward you for explaining effect, not just naming devices. Use this chain: technique, example, effect, link to meaning. For example, in an invented play where a bare stage holds one chair, you might write: "The empty set isolates the character, and the single chair suggests waiting and loneliness, which supports the theme of abandonment."

## Common mistakes
- Treating stage directions as if they were spoken lines.
- Confusing an aside (brief, others present) with a soliloquy (longer, alone).
- Confusing dramatic irony with verbal irony (saying the opposite of what you mean).
- Naming a technique without saying what it does.
- Describing the set or lighting without linking it to mood or theme.

## How this is examined
In an on-screen paper you are usually given a short script extract with stage directions, then asked a command-term question such as state, explain or analyse. A typical task asks you to explain how a playwright creates tension or reveals a character in a given scene. Multiple choice items may ask you to identify a technique, interpret a stage direction or choose the strongest analytical sentence. The best answers quote or refer closely to the extract, identify the technique and explain its effect on an audience.

Exam tip: Treat every bracket in a script extract as a clue, then write one sentence that names the technique, one that quotes it and one that explains its effect on the audience.

flashcards.back: A playwright's instruction about action, movement, setting, sound, lighting or delivery. It is not spoken aloud.
A speech by a character alone on stage that reveals private thoughts and feelings to the audience.
A brief remark a character makes to the audience while other characters are present but supposedly cannot hear it.
When the audience knows something that a character does not, creating tension, suspense or sympathy.
The unspoken meaning beneath the words, often shown through actions, pauses or tone.
A long speech by one character, usually addressed to other characters or the audience.
A movable object handled by actors on stage, such as a letter or a suitcase, often with symbolic meaning.
A voice outside the main action that comments on events, gives background and guides audience response.

flashcards.front: How should you analyse a dramatic technique?
flashcards.back: Name the technique, give an example from the extract, explain its effect on the audience, then link it to meaning or theme.

subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: What is dialogue in a play?
options: The spoken conversation between characters
The description of the set
The title of a scene
The costume list
questions.explanation: Dialogue is the words characters say to each other. It carries most of the information and conflict in a play.

questions.content: Which best defines conflict in drama?
options: A struggle between opposing characters, desires or forces
A scene that takes place in a courtroom
A long speech by one actor
The ending of the play
questions.explanation: Conflict is any opposition that drives the story, whether between people, within a character or between a character and society.

questions.content: A character wrestles with whether to tell the truth or protect a friend. What type of conflict is this?
options: Internal conflict
External conflict with nature
Conflict with technology
No conflict
questions.explanation: A struggle taking place inside a character's mind is an internal conflict.

questions.content: What does it mean to say a scene has tension?
options: The audience feels suspense or unease about what might happen
The characters are speaking quickly
The scene has many props
The lighting is very bright
questions.explanation: Tension is the feeling of suspense or unease that makes an audience wait to see how a conflict will resolve.

questions.content: What is a pause in a script usually used for?
options: To create silence that shows hesitation, tension or emotion
To tell the audience to leave
To end the play
To introduce a new character
questions.explanation: Pauses give moments for feelings to build without words, often increasing tension.

questions.content: Read this invented exchange. TESS: You were late again. RUBY: Traffic. TESS: Traffic. RUBY: Yes. What do the short, repeated replies suggest?
options: A guarded, strained relationship where little is said openly
A friendly, relaxed conversation
That Ruby is about to give a speech
That Tess does not speak English well
questions.explanation: Clipped one-word answers and echoing show reluctance and tension, with meaning left unspoken.

questions.content: In an invented scene, two brothers argue over who should look after their father's shop. One keeps interrupting the other. What is the most likely effect of the interruptions?
options: They show impatience and a struggle for control
They show the brothers agree on everything
They show the script has mistakes
They show that the scene is a flashback
questions.explanation: Interruptions on the page and on stage signal competition, frustration and an unwillingness to listen.

questions.content: A playwright writes lines that become shorter and faster as an argument builds. What effect does this create?
options: Rising pace and mounting tension
A calm, reflective mood
A sense of confusion about plot
A change of setting
questions.explanation: Shortening lines and quickening exchanges (sometimes called stichomythia) increases pace and intensity.

questions.content: In an invented scene, a mother says, "I'm not angry," while slamming a drawer shut. Which term best describes the effect?
options: Subtext: actions contradict the words
A soliloquy
A prologue
A stage whisper
questions.explanation: The gap between what she says and what she does is subtext, revealing her true feelings.

questions.content: Which feature most clearly shows a power imbalance in a dialogue between a manager and a new employee?
options: The manager gives orders and interrupts, while the employee apologises and asks permission
Both characters speak for the same length of time
Both characters laugh together
The employee is the one who sits down first
questions.explanation: Commands, interruptions and apologetic language show who holds authority. Equal turns and shared laughter suggest equality.

questions.content: In an invented play, a character says, "We should talk about the weather," right after an argument. What does this most probably suggest?
options: An attempt to avoid the real issue
A genuine interest in meteorology
That the play is set outdoors
That the argument has been resolved
questions.explanation: Changing to a trivial topic after conflict often shows avoidance, with the unspoken issue still hanging in the air.

questions.content: Which is an example of external conflict?
options: A villager defies the mayor who wants to close the school
A character feels guilty about a lie
A character cannot decide what to wear
A character remembers a happy day
questions.explanation: A struggle between a character and another person or force is external. Guilt and indecision are internal.

questions.content: In an invented scene, Ana asks, "Did you take the money?" and Leo answers, "Why would I take it?" What does answering a question with a question often reveal?
options: Evasion or defensiveness
Complete honesty
That Leo has not heard the question
That Ana is the villain
questions.explanation: Deflecting with another question avoids a direct answer, which can signal guilt or defensiveness, though it does not prove it.

questions.content: Read this invented extract. HANA: (quietly) You never said goodbye. DEV: I said I'd write. HANA: Did you? (A long pause.) DEV: I meant to. How does the writer build tension in the exchange?
options: By using short lines, a pause and an admission that leaves the conflict unresolved
By using long descriptions of scenery
By introducing a surprise character
By ending with a joke
questions.explanation: The brief lines, the pause and Dev's weak admission leave the audience aware of hurt that has not been resolved.

questions.content: A student claims, "The argument between the two sisters is just noise." Which counter-argument is strongest?
options: The argument reveals their competing loyalties and moves the plot by forcing a decision
Arguments are common in real life
The sisters are loud
Noise is needed in every play
questions.explanation: Strong reasoning ties the argument to character and plot function, not to surface description.

questions.content: In an invented play, a husband and wife discuss the price of a train ticket for several minutes, though the audience knows he plans to leave for good. What is the main effect?
options: Heightened tension, because the trivial talk masks and increases the unspoken crisis
Boredom, because nothing important is said
Confusion about the setting
A change of genre to farce
questions.explanation: Ordinary talk over a hidden crisis creates dramatic irony and subtext, so each mundane line carries added weight.

questions.content: In an invented scene, Priya answers each of Marcus's questions with exactly the same number of words, without ever looking at him. What does the playwright most probably wish to convey?
options: Controlled, defensive distance concealing strong emotion
That Priya enjoys the conversation
That Marcus is the stage manager
That the scene is a comedy about counting
questions.explanation: Measured replies and avoiding eye contact suggest deliberate control and withholding, a form of conflict through restraint.

questions.content: Which statement best explains why unresolved conflict at the end of a scene can be effective?
options: It leaves tension in the air and makes the audience anticipate the next scene
It proves that the writer ran out of ideas
It means no character has a goal
It stops the play from having a theme
questions.explanation: Leaving a conflict open sustains suspense and propels the audience forward. It is a deliberate structural choice.

note:
## Why dialogue matters
In a play, dialogue does several jobs at once. It reveals character, moves the plot forward, gives background information and creates tension. Unlike a novel, there is no narrator to explain what a person feels, so the audience must work out meaning from what is said, how it is said and what is left unsaid.

## Conflict
Conflict is the engine of drama. Without opposition, there is no story. Common kinds of conflict include:
- **Character against character**: two people want opposing things.
- **Internal conflict**: a character is torn between two choices or feelings.
- **Character against society or authority**: someone challenges rules or expectations.
- **Character against circumstance**: a storm, illness or poverty stands in the way.
A single scene often contains more than one kind. A teenager may argue with a parent (external) while privately doubting what they want (internal).

## How tension is built
Tension is the feeling of suspense or unease that makes an audience want to know what happens next. Playwrights create it through the shape of the dialogue:
- **Short, fast exchanges** increase pace, especially when lines get shorter as the argument builds.
- **Interruptions and overlapping speech** show impatience or a struggle for control.
- **Repetition** can show stubbornness or obsession.
- **Questions and evasions**: answering a question with a question often suggests defensiveness.
- **Silence and pauses** show what characters cannot or will not say.
- **Dramatic irony**: the audience knows more than a character, so every cheerful line feels risky.

## Subtext and power
Subtext is the real meaning underneath the words. A character who says "It's fine" while slamming a door is telling us the truth through action. Power can also be seen in dialogue: the person giving commands, interrupting, or choosing the topic usually holds control, while the person apologising or asking permission is weaker in that moment. Notice when the power shifts.

## Writing about dialogue
Use a simple pattern: **point** (what the dialogue shows), **evidence** (a short quotation), **effect** (what it does to the audience), **link** (how it connects to theme or character). For example, in an invented scene where two sisters share short, clipped replies: "The clipped lines show tension and hurt that neither will name. This makes the audience wait for the moment the argument finally breaks."

## Common mistakes
- Saying "they argue" without explaining what the argument reveals.
- Ignoring stage directions and pauses, which often carry the real feeling.
- Treating every word as literal and missing subtext.
- Quoting long chunks instead of short, precise evidence.
- Forgetting to explain the effect on the audience.

## How this is examined
On-screen papers often give you a short invented-style scene and ask you to explain how the writer creates conflict or tension, or to identify what a line suggests about a relationship. Multiple choice items may test whether you can recognise subtext, a power imbalance or the effect of short lines, and the strongest option is usually the one that links technique to effect.

Exam tip: When a question says "explain how tension is created", quote one short line, name the feature (for example a pause, interruption or evasion) and state exactly what feeling it creates in the audience.

flashcards.back: A struggle between opposing characters, desires or forces that drives the plot. It can be internal or external.
A struggle within a character's mind, such as a choice between duty and desire.
A struggle between a character and another person, society, authority or circumstance.
The feeling of suspense or unease that makes an audience anticipate what will happen next.
The unspoken meaning beneath the words, shown through actions, pauses and tone.
Rapid, short lines of dialogue traded between characters, which increase pace and show a heated argument.

flashcards.front: Signs of a power imbalance in dialogue
flashcards.back: Commands, interruptions, controlling the topic, and apologetic or permission-seeking language from the weaker speaker.

flashcards.front: Why use a pause in a script?
flashcards.back: To show hesitation, shock or unspoken feeling, and to build tension through silence.
Point, short quotation, effect on the audience, then link to character or theme.

subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: What does it mean to read a play "as performance"?
options: To imagine how it would look and sound on stage
To read only the stage directions
To memorise every line
To ignore the characters
questions.explanation: Reading as performance means picturing staging, voice, movement and audience reaction, because plays are written to be performed.

questions.content: Who is responsible for deciding how a play is interpreted on stage?
options: The director, working with actors and designers
The audience alone
The ticket seller
Only the printer of the script
questions.explanation: The director leads the interpretation, working with actors, designers and technicians to bring the script to life.

questions.content: Which of these is part of staging?
options: Where actors stand and move on the stage
The name of the playwright
The number of pages in the script
The date the play was printed
questions.explanation: Staging includes positioning, movement, set, lighting and sound.

questions.content: What does an actor's tone of voice contribute to a performance?
options: It shows emotion and attitude behind the words
It changes the script's spelling
It tells the audience the title
It replaces the set
questions.explanation: The same line can mean different things depending on how it is said, so tone conveys feeling and attitude.

questions.content: Which sentence is a performance-based observation about an invented script?
options: The actor could stand far from the other character to show emotional distance
The script has forty lines
The play is called Winter Door
The writer is from a small town
questions.explanation: Suggesting a staging choice and its effect is performance-based. The others are facts about the text that make no interpretive point.

questions.content: In an invented scene, a character says "Come in" in two ways: warmly while smiling, or flatly while looking at the floor. What does this show?
options: Delivery can change the meaning of the same words
The script must be rewritten
The character is two people
Words alone fix the meaning
questions.explanation: Delivery, including tone and body language, shapes interpretation of identical words.

questions.content: A director stages an argument with both actors sitting far apart on opposite sides of the stage. What effect might this create?
options: Emotional distance and a sense of division
Warmth and closeness
A sense that they are strangers who have never met
A comic mood only
questions.explanation: Physical distance on stage commonly symbolises emotional distance or division.

questions.content: In an invented production, a ghost appears in a cold blue light with a low humming sound. Which element is mainly creating atmosphere?
options: Lighting and sound together
The printed title
The page layout
The programme
questions.explanation: Colour and sound design shape mood. Blue light and low hum suggest coldness and the supernatural.

questions.content: A student writes that a character's costume changes from bright yellow to dark grey during the play. Which interpretation best fits?
options: It reflects a shift from hope to despair
It shows the budget got smaller
It shows the character changed their job
It has no effect on meaning
questions.explanation: Costume colour is a visual symbol. A move from bright to dark can mirror the character's changing fortunes.

questions.content: Which production choice would most strongly emphasise that a character is trapped?
options: Placing them inside a narrow pool of light surrounded by darkness
Allowing them to walk freely across the whole stage
Giving them a loud musical entrance
Having them wave at the audience
questions.explanation: Confined light visually restricts the character, suggesting entrapment.

questions.content: Why might two productions of the same play feel very different?
options: Directors and actors make different interpretive choices about staging, tone and design
The audience changes the script mid-show
Plays have no fixed text
Actors must always copy earlier productions
questions.explanation: The text stays the same but interpretation changes. Different choices lead to different effects and meanings.

questions.content: In an invented scene a character delivers a threat in a calm, quiet voice rather than shouting. What might the director want to show?
options: Controlled menace that can feel more frightening than anger
That the character is sleepy
That the microphone is broken
That the scene is comic
questions.explanation: A restrained delivery can seem more dangerous because it suggests control. Loudness is not the only way to show threat.

questions.content: A scene's stage direction says the characters stand at opposite ends of a long table. Which suggestion best uses this detail as performance evidence?
options: The table acts as a physical barrier that mirrors their strained relationship
Tables are normal in kitchens
It means the scene is in a kitchen
It means the actors have to eat
questions.explanation: A strong answer treats a staging detail as meaningful and links it to the relationship.

questions.content: In an invented production, the stage floor is covered in fallen paper for the final scene while the lights stay warm. A reviewer says it "looks messy". Which response best improves the point?
options: The scattered paper suggests lost plans or abandoned hopes, while the warm light gives the ending a gentle, forgiving tone
Paper is cheap
The floor should have been swept
Warm light is more flattering to actors
questions.explanation: Strong performance analysis explains how design choices combine to produce meaning, not just whether they look neat.

questions.content: A director wants the audience to see an overbearing father as sympathetic rather than villainous. Which choice would best support this?
options: Giving him moments of hesitation and a softened tone when he is alone
Having him shout all his lines
Lighting him in red whenever he enters
Keeping him offstage for the whole play
questions.explanation: Interpretation can reshape how an audience judges a character. Revealing vulnerability invites sympathy.

questions.content: Which statement shows the strongest understanding of the difference between text and performance?
options: The script gives words and directions, but a performance adds voice, movement, design and audience response, so meaning can shift
A performance is always identical to the script
Only the text matters
Performances never add meaning
questions.explanation: The strongest answer recognises that performance adds layers beyond the text and may change emphasis.

questions.content: Read this invented direction. (The stage is dark. A single phone rings six times. Nobody answers. The light rises to show an unmade bed and an empty glass.) How might a reader interpret the unanswered phone?
options: As evidence of absence, loneliness or something gone wrong, built through sound before the visual reveal
As proof the play is a comedy
As a mistake in the lighting plan
As a signal that the interval has begun
questions.explanation: The sound first creates anticipation and the unanswered ring, then the disordered room, build a picture of absence and unease.

questions.content: A student says a production "changed the play" by setting an invented palace drama in a modern office. Which is the most balanced evaluation?
options: The new setting can highlight power struggles in a familiar way, but it may lose some of the original period's meaning
Setting changes always ruin a play
Setting is never important
Modern settings are always better
questions.explanation: Balanced evaluation weighs gains and losses of an interpretive choice rather than treating it as simply good or bad.

note:
## Plays are written to be seen and heard
A novel can be fully enjoyed on the page, but a play script is incomplete until it is performed. Reading a play as performance means imagining it on stage: where characters stand, how they move, what the lighting does, how the voice sounds and how an audience reacts. In Language and Literature you are asked to explain meaning, and a performance lens helps you notice things you could easily miss on the page.

## The people and parts of a production
- **Playwright**: writes the script, including dialogue and stage directions.
- **Director**: decides the overall interpretation and guides the actors.
- **Actors**: bring characters to life through voice, expression, gesture and movement.
- **Designers**: create the set, costume, lighting and sound.
- **Audience**: completes the performance by reacting, laughing, gasping or staying silent.
The same text can produce very different productions because each team makes different choices.

## Elements to imagine
- **Voice**: tone, volume, speed and pauses. The same line, "I'm fine", can sound confident, hurt or sarcastic.
- **Body language and movement**: posture, gestures, facial expression, distance between characters. Standing close or far apart can show intimacy or division.
- **Use of space**: stage levels, entrances and exits, which character dominates the centre.
- **Set and props**: a bare set suggests emptiness or focus; a cluttered one suggests a crowded life.
- **Costume**: colour and condition suggest status and change. A coat that is too big may hint at insecurity.
- **Lighting**: bright light can feel safe or exposed, dim light mysterious, and a spotlight isolates.
- **Sound and music**: sudden sounds shock, quiet humming unsettles, and a cheerful song during sad moments can create ironic contrast.

## Making an interpretive argument
Because performance involves choice, you should frame your ideas as suggestions backed by evidence. Useful phrases include "A director might...", "This could be staged so that...", "The audience would probably feel...". Then link back to the text: a stage direction, a line, a pause. For example, in an invented scene in which two friends stand at opposite ends of a long table, you could write that the table works as a barrier that mirrors their strained friendship.

## Evaluating productions
You may be asked to evaluate a staging idea. Weigh the benefits and drawbacks. A modern setting for an old play might make the conflict easier to relate to, but could lose some original meaning. A balanced answer is stronger than one that simply says it is good or bad.

## Common mistakes
- Retelling the plot instead of discussing how the scene would work on stage.
- Listing set features without explaining their effect.
- Giving personal taste ("I would like this") rather than analysis.
- Treating performance choices as facts instead of possibilities backed by evidence.
- Forgetting that the audience's reaction is part of the performance.

## How this is examined
On-screen papers might give a script extract and ask how it could be staged to emphasise a feeling, or ask you to justify a staging choice. Multiple choice questions may ask you to choose the interpretation best supported by a stage direction, or to identify the strongest evaluative comment. Top answers use precise detail from the extract and explain effect on an audience.

Exam tip: When asked how to stage a moment, make one clear choice (voice, movement, lighting or set), justify it with a detail from the extract and state the effect it would have on the audience.
